\begin{proof} We first record the change of variables on the zero-sum hyperplane. Write
  $u_j = (x_j, t_j) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}$. Set
  \[ u_{d + 2} = (- z, - v), \qquad u_i = (w_i z + a_i, w_i v), \qquad 1 \leq
     i \leq d + 1. \]
  Then
  \[ \sum_{j = 1}^{d + 2} u_j = 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \sum_{i =
     1}^{d + 1} a_i = 0, \qquad \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1} w_i = 1. \]
  Indeed,
  \[ \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1} u_i = \left( \left( \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1} w_i \right)
     z + \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1} a_i,  \left( \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1}
     w_i \right) v \right), \]
  and this is equal to $(z, v) = - u_{d + 2}$ precisely under the two
  displayed constraints.

  The Jacobian factor is $|v|^d$. One way to see this without choosing
  coordinates on the constrained hyperplanes is the following. Put $x_i = w_i
  z + a_i$ and $t_i = w_i v$. The change $a_i \mapsto x_i$ has determinant
  $1$, while $w_i \mapsto t_i = w_i v$ contributes $|v|^{- (d + 1)}$.
  Moreover,
  \[ \delta_0  \left( \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1} w_i - 1 \right) = |v| 
      \delta_0  \left( \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1} t_i - v \right), \]
  and
  \[ \delta_0 \left( \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1} a_i \right) = \delta_0  \left(
     \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1} x_i - z \right) \]
  on the hyperplane $\sum_i w_i = 1$. Thus the factor $|v|^d$ converts the
  constrained measure in the variables $(a_i, w_i, z, v)$ into the measure
  \[ \delta_0 \left( \sum_{j = 1}^{d + 2} u_j \right)  \prod_{j = 1}^{d + 2}
     \dd u_j . \]
  It remains to compute the determinant. Add the first $d + 1$ columns of the
  affine determinant matrix to the last column. Since $\sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1}
  u_i = (z, v)$ and $u_{d + 2} = (- z, - v)$, the last column becomes $(0,
  \ldots, 0, d + 2)^T$. Expanding along this column gives
  \[ D^{(d+1)} (u_1, \ldots, u_{d + 2}) = (d + 2) \det (u_1, \ldots, u_{d +
     1}) . \]
  Now
  \[ \det (u_1, \ldots, u_{d + 1}) = \det \left( \begin{matrix}
       a_1 + w_1 z & \cdots & a_{d + 1} + w_{d + 1} z\\
       w_1 v & \cdots & w_{d + 1} v
     \end{matrix} \right) . \]
  Subtracting $z / v$ times the last row from the first $d$ rows, and then
  factoring $v$ from the last row, gives, for $v \neq 0$,
  \[ \det (u_1, \ldots, u_{d + 1}) = v \det \left( \begin{matrix}
       a_1 & \cdots & a_{d + 1}\\
       w_1 & \cdots & w_{d + 1}
     \end{matrix} \right) . \]
  The same identity holds for all $v$ by polynomial continuation. Since
  $\sum_i a_i = 0$, the determinant in the last display is a linear function
  of the final row which vanishes on $\{\rho \in \mathbb{R}^{d + 1} : \sum_i
  \rho_i = 0\}$. Therefore, using $\sum_i w_i = 1$,
  \[ \det \left( \begin{matrix}
       a_1 & \cdots & a_{d + 1}\\
       w_1 & \cdots & w_{d + 1}
     \end{matrix} \right) = \frac{1}{d + 1} \det \left( \begin{matrix}
       a_1 & \cdots & a_{d + 1}\\
       1 & \cdots & 1
     \end{matrix} \right) = \frac{1}{d + 1} D^{(d)} (a_1, \ldots, a_{d + 1})
     . \]
  Hence
  \[ D^{(d+1)} (u_1, \ldots, u_{d + 2}) = \frac{d + 2}{d + 1}  \hspace{0.17em}
     v  D^{(d)} (a_1, \ldots, a_{d + 1}), \]
  which is the determinant appearing in the stated formula. Substituting the
  change of variables and the determinant identity into the regularized form
  proves the claim. The distributional statement follows by passing to the
  regularized limit.
\end{proof}
